performers: Hans Duhan, baritone; Ferdinand Foll, piano
question: What can a song say when the music hardly moves?
intro: The cycle ends not in a climax but beside a beggar who plays a hurdy-gurdy for no one. Over a drone that hardly changes, the singer sees himself in the old man and asks to go with him.

sections.label: Introduction · the drone and the crank
Verses 1–2 · the old man and his plate
Interlude · four bars for the piano alone

cues.title: A drone and a turning figure
cues.text: The original score, in A minor, is marked Etwas langsam, in 3/4, with no sharps or flats. In eight bars for the piano alone, a low open fifth drones in the left hand while quick figures turn above it, like a hurdy-gurdy’s cranked wheel and its drone strings. The voice enters at about 0:22.
cues.evidence: The marking, the 3/4 metre, the empty key signature of the original A-minor score (the recording sounds lower, so the printed signature is not its pitch), the open fifth held in the left hand and the quick right-hand figures of bars 1–8 are in the OpenScore transcription (CC0); a boundary at 0:16 (novelty 0.62) and one at 0:22 (0.34) bracket the entry in bar 9, which is proportioned from the score’s bars. The level is −22.2 dB at 0:00.

cues.title: Phrases and answers
cues.text: The voice enters at about 0:22 and sings two-bar phrases over the drone. In the first verse the piano’s turning figure answers in the gaps between them.
cues.evidence: Boundaries at 0:16 (0.62) and 0:22 (0.34). In the score the voice enters in bar 9 and sings its two-bar phrases in bars 9–10 and 13–14 over the drone, with a right-hand chord added in bar 13, while the turning figure fills the gaps in bars 11–12 and 15–16 (OpenScore); times are proportioned.

cues.title: A hurdy-gurdy man
cues.text: Over there, behind the village, a hurdy-gurdy man turns his crank with numb fingers, as best he can. A hurdy-gurdy sounds by a cranked, rosined wheel and has drone strings; the Germans called it the Bettlerleier, the beggar’s lyre.
cues.evidence: Wilhelm Müller, Die Winterreise, no. 24, first stanza (Wikisource, https://de.wikisource.org/wiki/Die_Winterreise_(Müller)), paraphrased, sung in bars 9–16 of the score (OpenScore). Wikipedia’s Hurdy-gurdy article (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurdy-gurdy), lead and History: the cranked wheel, the drone strings, and the German names Bauernleier and Bettlerleier.

cues.title: No one listens
cues.text: Barefoot on the ice he totters to and fro, and his little plate stays always empty. No one wants to hear him, no one looks at him, and the dogs growl around the old man. Schubert sets the plate’s couplet twice.
cues.evidence: Wilhelm Müller, Die Winterreise, no. 24, second and third stanzas (Wikisource, https://de.wikisource.org/wiki/Die_Winterreise_(Müller)), paraphrased. They are sung in bars 17–38 of the score (OpenScore), from 46.5 s (bar 17) in the aligned score to about 1:56; the plate couplet “Und sein kleiner Teller bleibt ihm immer leer” is set twice, in bars 21–22 and 25–26.

cues.title: The piano alone
cues.text: Between about 1:20 and 1:32 the voice rests and the piano plays four bars alone. Listen for the drone and the little figure: the machine keeps turning with nobody to hear it. The level dips at about 1:25.
cues.evidence: The level is −25.0 dB at 1:25 with 0.8 attacks per second, one of the quieter windows before the closing decay; a boundary at 1:32 (0.34) follows. The score has no voice in bars 27–30 and the verse resumes at bar 31 (OpenScore); times are proportioned.

cues.title: The wheel never stops
cues.text: He lets everything happen as it will. He turns the crank, and his hurdy-gurdy never stands still. The last couplet is sung twice.
cues.evidence: Wilhelm Müller, Die Winterreise, no. 24, fourth stanza (Wikisource, https://de.wikisource.org/wiki/Die_Winterreise_(Müller)), paraphrased. It is sung in bars 39–48 of the score, its last couplet in bars 43–44 and again in 47–48 (OpenScore), about 1:58–2:26 by proportion.

cues.title: The last silence, then the question
cues.text: After the fourth verse comes four bars of piano alone, a very quiet stretch at about 2:30 and 2:35. Then, at about 2:41, the voice turns to its last question. Its final line leaps an octave and falls on the loudest window of the song, at 2:55.
cues.evidence: The windows at 2:30 and 2:35 are very quiet (−24.5 and −25.4 dB), with 1:25 (−25.0 dB) and 3:05 (−26.2 dB) similar before the final decay; boundaries at 2:34 (0.37) and 2:42 (0.31). The strongest boundary is 2:52 (novelty 1.00) and the loudest 5-second window is 2:55 (−7.1 dB, 3.8 attacks per second). In the score the voice rests in bars 49–52 and the question begins at bar 53, 161.4 s in the aligned score, its last line leaping from E4 to E5 (OpenScore); the times before bar 53 are proportioned.

cues.title: Shall I go with you?
cues.text: Strange old man, he asks, shall I go with you? Will you turn your hurdy-gurdy to my songs?
cues.evidence: Wilhelm Müller, Die Winterreise, no. 24, fifth stanza (Wikisource, https://de.wikisource.org/wiki/Die_Winterreise_(Müller)), paraphrased. It is sung in bars 53–58 of the score, the last note tied into bar 58 (OpenScore), from 161.4 s in the aligned score.

cues.title: Schubert’s last proofs
cues.text: Schubert’s last task in life was correcting the proofs of the second part of Winterreise, days before he died on 19 November 1828. Haslinger published it on 30 December. The piano returns to its opening figure and ends on a plain minor chord in the score, giving no answer.
cues.evidence: Wikipedia’s Winterreise article (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winterreise), “Authorship and composition” and “Legacy”: the proofs, Schubert’s death on 19 November and publication on 30 December 1828. The score repeats the opening figure in bars 58–60 and ends on an A minor chord in bar 61 (OpenScore); a boundary at 2:58 (0.43) and silence from 3:10 are in the report.

transitions.title: The drone waits, then a voice
transitions.from: Introduction · the drone and the crank
transitions.to: Verses 1–2 · the old man and his plate
transitions.how: Eight bars for the piano alone establish the open fifth in the left hand and a turning figure above it, in an original A-minor score with no key signature. The voice enters in bar 9 and sings two-bar phrases over the drone; in the first verse the right hand’s turning figure fills the gaps between them. The singer joins an instrument that is already running.
transitions.evidence: Boundaries at 0:16 (0.62) and 0:22 (0.34). The score has no voice in bars 1–8 and the open fifth A–E in the left hand throughout the song (OpenScore); the entry time is proportioned.

transitions.title: Four bars of piano, then no listeners
transitions.from: Verses 1–2 · the old man and his plate
transitions.how: After the plate couplet is sung twice, the voice rests and the piano plays four bars alone: the drone and the turning figure, with a few added notes in the left hand. Then the third verse enters at about 1:32 over the same fifth. Two-bar rests already separate the voice’s phrases; this rest lasts four bars and the piano fills it with its own figure. The drone and the basic texture carry on: only the voice is absent.
transitions.evidence: The level is −21.5 dB at 1:20 and −25.0 dB at 1:25 (0.8 attacks per second); boundaries at 1:20 (0.32) and 1:32 (0.34). The score has no voice in bars 27–30 and the third verse begins at bar 31 (OpenScore), at 92.3 s in the aligned score; the interlude starts at about 1:20 by proportion.

transitions.title: The fourth verse ends, the voice rests
transitions.to: Interlude · four bars for the piano alone
transitions.how: The fourth verse ends with its last couplet sung twice, and the voice rests again for four bars. The piano plays the drone and the turning figure alone, with the short added line in the left hand, as in the first interlude. The level falls to a very quiet stretch, at about 2:30 and 2:35.
transitions.evidence: The level is −24.5 dB at 2:30 and −25.4 dB at 2:35; boundaries at 2:34 (0.37) and 2:42 (0.31). The score has no voice in bars 49–52 (OpenScore); the interlude starts at about 2:29 by proportion.

transitions.title: Four bars of piano, then the question
transitions.from: Interlude · four bars for the piano alone
transitions.how: After the interlude the voice enters again over the same drone with its last verse, the question: shall I go with you? The drone and the basic texture have carried on for 150 seconds; what changes is the singer’s address, from description to a request. The last line leaps an octave and falls on the loudest window of the song, at about 2:55.
transitions.evidence: The question begins at bar 53, 161.4 s in the aligned score (OpenScore); boundaries at 2:42 (0.31) and the strongest boundary of the song at 2:52 (1.00), with the loudest window at 2:55 (−7.1 dB).

transitions.title: The opening figure returns
transitions.how: The voice ends its question at the loudest window of the song, near 2:55, and holds its last note while the piano begins the figure of its introduction again. The piano alone then plays the last three bars and stops on a plain minor chord in the score, without a cadence that answers. The drone that began the song also ends it. The recording falls from −17.0 dB at 3:00 to silence by 3:10, and the question stays open.
transitions.evidence: The strongest boundary is 2:52 (1.00); a boundary at 2:58 (0.43); level −7.1 dB at 2:55, −17.0 dB at 3:00, −26.2 dB at 3:05 and silence at 3:10. The score repeats the opening figure in bars 58–60 and ends on a minor chord in bar 61 over the drone (OpenScore); times are proportioned.

fields.label: Performers
fields.note: The label photograph of the scanned copy names Kammersänger Hans Duhan, baritone of the Vienna State Opera, with Prof. Ferdinand Foll at the piano; the Internet Archive description names the same two performers. Utz reports that Duhan recorded nineteen songs with Foll on 27 April, 2 May and 4 May 1928 and the remaining five (Nos. 16, 17, 19, 20, 23) with Lene Orthmann on 11 July 1928, so Orthmann does not play on this side. The Commons file description names only Duhan.

fields.label: Work version
fields.note: Utz measures this song at 3:10 against a mean of 3:41 and describes a clear slowing in its second part. No source consulted states the key of the transfer; the transposition from the first edition and the absolute pitch are not established here.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: The Internet Archive description of the disc that carries this side gives the recording date. Utz lists the same three Foll session days (27 April, 2 May and 4 May 1928) without assigning songs to days, so the song-by-day assignment rests on the Internet Archive uploader’s labelling. Commons gives only the year 1928.

fields.label: Place
fields.note: No source consulted names the studio or city of the session.

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Gramola Record (The Gramophone Company (Czechoslovakia) Limited), as printed on the scanned copy
fields.note: The label photograph of this scanned copy shows a Gramola Record imprint, whereas the photographed first disc carries the His Master’s Voice imprint; the photographed copies of this set carry both imprints. The label gives no date, and nothing here dates the first issue or shows that the audio transfer derives from the photographed copy.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: The label photograph of the scanned copy prints Cat. No. ER 276, and the Commons file name agrees. The Internet Archive text description of the disc reads “ER 376”, which the photograph does not support; the discrepancy is the uploader’s.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.value: BK 2969, take 1 (run-out “Bk 2969” with I); side No. 24 (label number 942922); reverse side: Die Nebensonnen (matrix CL 4401-1; pianist Lene Orthmann, 11 July 1928). Disc 12 of 12 of the set; 25 cm.
fields.note: The label photograph of the scanned copy shows the matrix and take in the run-out; the Internet Archive description and the Commons file name give the same matrix and take. The set was issued as twelve discs, one song to a side (Utz). The photograph is of one copy and does not identify the copy from which the audio was transferred.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.note: No transfer engineer is named. The Commons file was uploaded on 11 August 2015 by the user Patachonf and re-uploaded on 10 and 15 February 2022 by the user Mitar; the Internet Archive item was added on 25 April 2019 by the uploader recordplayer78. These are upload facts, not transfer credits.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: No transfer date is identified. Upload dates are not treated as transfer dates.

fields.label: Processing
fields.note: Both hosts hold a FLAC file. The Commons duration (195.50 s) and the Internet Archive FLAC length (195.41 s) agree within 0.15 s, which suggests the same digitisation; which host received it first is not established, and the source disc, stylus, equalisation and noise treatment are undocumented.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Both the music and the poem are out of copyright where the ordinary life-plus-70 term applies.
fields.note: Schubert died in 1828 and the poet Wilhelm Müller in 1827. This is a term calculation, not a worldwide clearance or a statement about any modern edition.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Rule 3 — territorial: sound recording public domain in the European Union (pre-1963 publication basis).
fields.note: Commons applies PD-EU-audio to this recording, attributed to 1928. The Internet Archive item carries a Creative Commons Public Domain Mark 1.0 licence URL, which is the uploader’s assertion and is not treated as authority to waive any rights. The publication date of the original disc is not documented; the EU basis here depends on the recording being first published before 1963, which is inferred from its 1928 session. Not established as public domain in the United States.

composer.epithet: A Viennese songwriter who made the piano an equal narrator, and carried the harmonic dislocations of the Lied into symphonies and chamber music.
facts: Vienna Stadtkonvikt, 1808–13; composition with Antonio Salieri, 1812–16
Assistant in his father’s school; music tutor to the Esterházy family at Zseliz in 1818 and 1824; thereafter chiefly an independent composer
Johann Michael Vogl · Josef von Spaun · Franz von Schober · Johann Mayrhofer · Moritz von Schwind
More than 600 songs; symphonies, chamber music, piano sonatas and duets, masses and music for the stage
composer.background:
Schubert grew up in a schoolmaster’s household in Himmelpfortgrund, then a suburb of Vienna. His father taught him violin, his brother Ignaz taught him piano, and the parish musician Michael Holzer supplied further instruction. Family quartet sessions put Franz on viola, between the melody and the bass: he knew chamber music from an inner part. In 1808 he entered the imperial chapel choir and the Stadtkonvikt boarding school. Its orchestra introduced him to Haydn, Mozart and Beethoven as a player, while Antonio Salieri began giving him composition lessons in 1812.

After leaving the school in 1813, he trained as a teacher and became an assistant in his father’s classroom. Composition continued around the timetable. Gretchen am Spinnrade, dated 19 October 1814, gives Goethe’s girl a right-hand spinning wheel, a left-hand treadle and a vocal line that repeatedly tries to escape them. Schubert was seventeen. In 1815 he wrote roughly 140 songs, including Erlkönig, as well as symphonies, church music and stage works. Voice and piano already carried distinct dramatic responsibilities in his songs.
